note: The canonical instrument list. A review works through it in order and must account for every id, every pass. It is meant to GROW: when a pass finds something by a technique not listed here, that technique is added as a row before the review ends, so the next review starts where this one finished instead of re-inventing it. The hook checks that every finding names the instrument that found it, and that the name resolves to a row in this file.

instruments.name: Scope the change
instruments.asks: Which files changed, and which boundaries do they cross?

instruments.name: Read prior ledgers
instruments.asks: Has this area already been reviewed, and what was already found and fixed?

instruments.name: Print the built string or payload
instruments.trigger: a prompt, request, or message is assembled
instruments.asks: What does the consumer actually receive? Print it for at least TWO materially different inputs -- the dimensions the code actually branches on: man and woman, empty and full, anime and realistic, first render and retry. One input proves the literal is spelled right and nothing else. Every likeness prompt in this repository was printed five times across two reviews, always with a woman, while every sentence after the subject line was hardcoded to "She is wearing" and "Her top" -- so a male character was described as a woman for as long as the feature existed, in an artifact a review had read five times.

instruments.name: Print the rendered markup
instruments.asks: What is on the screen, including what a screen reader gets?

instruments.name: Print the HTTP body
instruments.asks: What does the client actually receive, status and body?

instruments.name: Print the SQL, plan, or stored row
instruments.asks: What is actually written and read back?

instruments.name: Match constants across the seam
instruments.asks: Do both sides spell every code, key and enum the same?

instruments.name: Match the shape the caller receives
instruments.asks: Is the field the caller reads the field the sender sets?

instruments.name: Differential run of two implementations
instruments.trigger: one rule lives in two places
instruments.asks: Do they agree on the same inputs, and what stops them drifting?

instruments.name: Contract with the worker or provider
instruments.trigger: the worker or an external contract changed
instruments.asks: Does the other end do what this end assumes?

instruments.name: Is the field wired, or only declared?
instruments.trigger: a field is added to a struct that crosses a boundary
instruments.asks: Is the (de)serialiser generated or hand-written? A hand-written decoder, scanner, encoder or column list ignores struct tags, so a field added without a line there is populated by nothing while reading as correct. Find the function that actually moves the bytes and check the new field appears in it -- then check every sibling path the field beside it already had: decode, bound, persist, log.

instruments.name: Mutate the accessor, not just the field
instruments.trigger: a value crosses a boundary through an untyped map, a reflection read, a hand-written decoder, or any accessor that can fail silently
instruments.asks: Break the READER and see whether anything fails. A wiring test that only checks what the writer produced leaves the read unguarded, and a type assertion that no longer matches returns a zero value rather than an error. Changing intField from .(int) to .(int64) turned every hosted clip's duration into zero and the entire queue suite still passed -- the key check proved the key was present and the builder's type was right, and said nothing about the read. The fix is a round-trip assertion: build the real thing, read it back through the real accessor, and require that nothing came back zero.

instruments.name: Does the fixture match what the producer really emits?
instruments.trigger: a test supplies a value that some other code produces in production -- a path, a filename, an id, a header, a payload
instruments.asks: Build the value the way production builds it, not the way that is convenient to type. downloadGeneratedMedia writes to os.CreateTemp and decides the file type afterwards by sniffing the bytes, so every real download landed on a path with NO extension -- while every test handed the same code a file called artifact.mp4. ffmpeg picks its output container from the output name, so the playback rendition produced an unnamed output and failed on every real render, silently, with a green suite. The fixture was not wrong about the content; it was wrong about the shape, in the one attribute the code under test actually read. Find the function that mints the value in production and mint it the same way in the test, or assert the shape explicitly.

instruments.name: Probe with real inputs that must pass
instruments.asks: Does it accept the things people really type?

instruments.name: Probe with hostile inputs that must fail
instruments.asks: Does it refuse the thing it exists to refuse?

instruments.name: Probe the boundaries
instruments.asks: Empty, max, max plus one, unicode, whitespace, control characters?

instruments.name: What do siblings set that this does not?
instruments.asks: Which defence do neighbouring paths carry that this path lost?

instruments.name: What branch is now unreachable?
instruments.asks: Can every branch still be reached by some real input?

instruments.name: What error is swallowed?
instruments.asks: Does every failure reach somebody who can act on it?

instruments.name: What is gated on a flag this path lacks?
instruments.asks: Which conditional excludes this path without saying so?

instruments.name: What is duplicated that should be one?
instruments.asks: Which constant, rule or literal now exists twice?

instruments.name: Where else does this shape occur?
instruments.trigger: any finding, before it is written down
instruments.asks: A defect is a shape, and a repository rarely has one instance of a shape. Having found one, grep for every other place that makes or reads the same kind of value and ask the same question there. The download path named a temp file before it knew the file type, so the name had no extension and ffmpeg could not choose a container -- and resolveMediaSource, written by somebody else for a different job, does exactly the same thing, so the shipped thumbnail job could never make a video thumbnail for anything stored remotely. One was found by a test; the second was found only by looking for it. Do this while the shape is still in your head, because after the fix is committed nobody looks again.

instruments.name: Race detector
instruments.trigger: a goroutine or shared state changed
instruments.asks: Does it still pass under -race?

instruments.name: Transaction, lock order, partial failure
instruments.asks: What happens when it fails half way?

instruments.name: Migration ladder and rollback
instruments.asks: Is every ladder updated, and does every up have a down?

instruments.name: Delete, cancel, re-do and orphan paths
instruments.asks: What is left behind when this is undone?

instruments.name: Control every fix
instruments.asks: Does the new test fail when the fix is reverted? Then print the artifact the fix changed, once more, before closing. Review-time code is the least reviewed code in the repository: it is written last, quickly, under the urge to be finished. A rewrite made during one review put "unadorned at the neck, ears and wrists" into a head-and-shoulders prompt -- naming a body part the crop excludes -- and every portrait came back as a three-quarter body shot until somebody rendered one.

instruments.name: Is the guard reachable?
instruments.trigger: a check, guard, hook or script exists to prevent something
instruments.asks: What invokes it automatically? Grep for its name outside its own file and its own tests. A guard nobody runs is not a weaker guard, it is no guard: this repository has one that correctly refuses tracked build artifacts and was referenced only by its own test suite, and a 79 MB binary was committed four commits after it was written. Assert the wiring in the guard's own tests, beside the behaviour, because 'correct but unreachable' is invisible to every test of the behaviour.

instruments.name: Gates
instruments.asks: Do build, vet, lint, types and tests pass?

instruments.name: What did this pass do that the list does not name?
instruments.asks: Which technique found it, and is that technique a row here yet? If not, add it.

instruments.name: Run it against the real thing and compare the outputs to each other
instruments.trigger: anything whose output is produced by a model, a provider, or another system
instruments.asks: Not just: is each output correct? Also: are the outputs different from each other in the ways the feature promises, and does anyone looking at them agree they are what was asked for? This may NOT be marked na because it costs money or GPU time. If a prompt or any other model input changed and nothing has been rendered since, that is a finding with no fix yet: record it as an explicit unverified row and say so to the user, rather than burying it among twenty other na lines. Applied once in the first 23 passes and skipped fifteen times -- and meanwhile every product defect that actually reached a picture was found by running it, none of them by a review.

instruments.name: Does anything start before the decision that governs it?
instruments.trigger: work is kicked off early to save time -- a prefetch, a stream, a subscription, a goroutine
instruments.asks: Find every side effect started before a later branch decides whether it was wanted, and ask what happens on the branch that did not want it. Cancelling afterwards is not enough when the side effect is not undoable. A call started its sentence playback at the top of the turn, to overlap synthesis with generation; the choice of whether the AVATAR speaks the reply is made further down, after the reply arrives -- so in video mode she was heard twice, once from the local speaker and once from the avatar's stream, half a beat apart, and the cancel that followed could not unsay the words already spoken. Speech, sends, writes and payments are all in this class: pull the decision earlier, or do not start early on that branch.

instruments.name: Does the guard refuse a known-bad input?
instruments.trigger: a check, guard, CI step or hook exists to refuse something
instruments.asks: Feed it the thing it exists to refuse, and require it to refuse. A guard can be wired in, run on every push, and check nothing: CI's 'TypeScript type check' ran `tsc --noEmit` against a root tsconfig with "files": [], so it checked an empty project and passed every run for months, type errors and all. It was found by adding a file containing `const x: number = 'a'` and running CI's exact command: exit 0. G2 asks whether anything runs the guard; this asks whether the guard, when it runs, sees anything. Take the command from where it really runs (the workflow file, the hook), not from memory, and keep the known-bad probe as a test so a later edit cannot blind it again.

instruments.name: Measure the rendered layout at the narrowest real widths
instruments.trigger: a component changed what sits in a shared bar, header, toolbar or row
instruments.asks: Open the real page in a real browser at 360, 375 and 390 px and at a desktop width, put the real rendered markup in place for every state the change adds (and the worst realistic content: the longest balance, name, timer and message), and measure: does the row scroll, does any control overlap another, does any text overflow its own box, does anything grow taller than its bar? jsdom has no layout, so every class-level test passes while the header is broken. B2 added call controls to the OmniChat header; every test was green and the row needed 444 px on a 360 px phone -- mute over the logo, the exit off screen. The first fix was measured with the signed-out account button (52 px, not the signed-in 78 px) and still overlapped; a box-overlap check then missed the logo text spilling out of a shrunk box. Measure boxes AND text overflow (scrollWidth > clientWidth), signed in, with the longest content.

instruments.name: What changes the process-wide state that lazy code reads?
instruments.trigger: code reads process-wide state on first use and caches it: the working directory, environment variables, the clock, a global, a sync.Once
instruments.asks: Find everything in the same process that can change that state before the first read, and ask what the cached value becomes when it runs first. A lazily-read value is correct only for the order in which the tests happen to run today; -run, -shuffle or one new file changes the order. TestDSN named each package test database after the working directory on the first NewTest() call -- and a handlers test calls t.Chdir(t.TempDir()), so whenever it ran first the whole handlers binary would have been named after a temp directory like 001, possibly one shared with another package, which is exactly the cross-package collision the change existed to remove. Read the state once, before any test can run (a package-level variable), or pass it in.

instruments.name: Did the tests run, or skip?
instruments.trigger: a gate or a control reports a test as passing, and that test can skip -- on a missing variable, an unreachable service, a failed connection
instruments.asks: Run it with -v and count PASS against SKIP; 'ok' is printed for a package whose every test skipped. Then find every skip condition in the tests the change touches and ask whether CI meets it. In one session 'ok' came three times from skipped tests: all sixteen changed integration tests (TEST_DATABASE_URL unset locally), the workers database test inside a timed full run reported as proof the database was created, and security's SQL injection test, which dialled a user CI does not have and skipped on every run since it was written. Given a real database it failed four subtests on assumptions nobody had ever checked. A test that always skips is not a weak test; it is no test, and the suite stays green around it.

instruments.name: Does the change keep every promise of the approved plan?
instruments.trigger: the change is one phase of a plan the user approved
instruments.asks: Reread the plan's own sentences for this phase and check each against the code: every 'deletes', 'never', 'only' and 'at once' is a guarantee someone will rely on without looking. The login-key plan said the move to the new scheme 'deletes the password copy'; the first cut of the move changed only the login columns, so the private key copy wrapped with a password the server had seen would have stayed on the server for good. Nothing in the diff was wrong on its own terms, and no test asked, because the test was written from the code rather than from the plan.

instruments.name: Can two entry points run the same side effect at once?
instruments.trigger: a side effect (making keys, a payment, an upload) is started from more than one place: an app-open check, a callback page, a retry, a second tab
instruments.asks: List every caller that can start it, and find a real page load or user path where two of them fire together. Run them together in a test with the first held open, and require the effect to happen once and the result to stay consistent. A guard on each caller alone does not see the other caller.

instruments.name: Is the layer on top of every layer that can open with it?
instruments.trigger: a component draws a fixed overlay, modal or full-screen step
instruments.asks: List every z-index and portal in the app (grep z-[ and createPortal), put the highest one that can open at the same time behind the new layer in a real browser, and ask elementFromPoint what is on top at the centre. A layer that must never be covered needs to sit above all of them, and outside any root it makes inert.

instruments.name: Run every test that mocks or imports a changed module
instruments.trigger: a module's exports, signature or behavior changed
instruments.asks: grep every test file in the package for the module's import path and for vi.mock of it, and run all of them, not only the tests beside the change. A narrow run passes while a distant integration test that mocks the old shape fails in CI; AuthContext's change broke tests/integration/authFlows.test.tsx for five pushes that way.

termination: A review is not one pass. It repeats until a full pass over every instrument finds nothing. A pass that finds something is evidence the previous pass was not finished -- the fix is new code nobody has reviewed, and the technique that found it may find more. There is no iteration budget: if it takes twenty passes, it takes twenty passes.
